description: Direct checks of the terrain horizon against dated images of the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC): is a given point sunlit or in shadow at the time of the image? Two cases, fixed before the image of case B was downloaded and before the core was run on either. Image times and geometry are those printed on the LROC data pages on 14 November 2026.
rule: Committed before any computation for these cases and before the image file of case B was downloaded. Not edited afterwards. If a check fails, the cause is looked for and reported; the criteria stay.

our_state.definition: At the point, on the surface (observer height 0 m), at the middle of the image exposure: 'sunlit' if at least half of the Sun's disc is above the terrain horizon (visible fraction >= 0.5), otherwise 'shadow'. Terrain: the LOLA products the tool uses (20 m near the pole), horizon to 300 km at 0.25 degree azimuth step.
our_state.why_half: Between the first and the last light the surface brightens gradually; half of the disc is the middle of that transition and the natural place to cut it into two states.
our_state.also_reported: visible fraction, margins of the upper limb and of the centre, azimuth of the Sun, elevation and distance of the terrain that limits it

lroc_featured_1276.title: LROC featured image 'Where is the South Pole?', M. Robinson, 19 October 2022

lroc_pds_M1407524099LE.title: LROC data page of NAC image M1407524099LE

lroc_pds_M146846913LE.title: LROC data page of NAC image M146846913LE

cases.kind: state documented by the camera team
cases.image: NAC M1407524099 (left and right frames), oblique view of the rim of Shackleton crater

published.statement: The featured-image page marks the south pole (90 S, 0 E), just inside the rim of Shackleton crater, with an arrow and describes it as 'now in shadows' and 'just into the shadows'.
published.precision: time to the second; sub-solar point printed to 0.01 degree; the state is a statement of the camera team, not a measurement by us

checks.criterion: our state at the south pole at 2022-05-18T14:40:49 UTC is 'shadow'
our sub-solar latitude and longitude at that time differ from the printed values by less than 0.02 degree each (0.005 degree is the rounding of the printed values)

cases.kind: state read from the image by a fixed rule
cases.image: NAC M146846913L, nadir view (emission angle 1.7 degrees) across the south pole, read from the calibrated browse pyramid M146846913LC_pyr.tif

published.precision: time to the second; corner coordinates printed to 0.01 degree, which is 300 m in latitude

protocol.georeferencing: Image position (fraction of lines, fraction of samples) is mapped to polar stereographic x, y by bilinear interpolation between the four printed corners; 'upper' is the first line, 'left' the first sample. No camera model is used.
protocol.points: Three rows along the strip: on the centre line and 700 m to either side of it, one point every 500 m from 1 km inside the first line to 1 km inside the last line.
protocol.image_state: The browse image is averaged to about 20 m per pixel. The brightness threshold is Otsu's threshold of that reduced image. A point is 'sunlit' in the image if every reduced pixel within 300 m of it is above the threshold, 'shadow' if every one is below, and 'mixed' otherwise. Mixed points are not judged: with corners known to 300 m, a point near a shadow edge cannot be read.

checks.criterion: among the judged points, our state agrees with the image state for at least 90 percent; at least 30 points must be judged and both states must occur among them, otherwise the case is reported as not decided
our sub-solar latitude and longitude at that time differ from the printed values by less than 0.02 degree each

cases.why_90_percent: Corners are known to 300 m and the transition from shadow to light is gradual; points within 300 m of an edge are already left out, so the remaining disagreements should be rare.

limits_known_in_advance: Case A rests on the camera team's own reading of its image; the pole lies close to the edge of the shadow ('just into the shadows'), so a small error of the horizon can flip our state.
Case B reads a lossy browse product with corner-based georeferencing; it can only test broad sunlit and shadowed areas, not the position of a shadow edge.
Two images, both near Shackleton crater.
